profile.name: Angloise
profile.tagline: Continental court adaptation of the English country dance set.
profile.insight: Carried to the court of Louis XIV in 1684, the Angloise merged English country sets with French baroque stepping, inspiring Mozart and Beethoven.
profile.profile: The Angloise, also known as the Anglais or contredanse anglaise, is the French and Continental European adaptation of the English country dance. Arriving at the court of Louis XIV in 1684, it synthesised British figures with French courtly styling and footwork. Danced in formations such as longways sets and squares, it relied on progressive figures executed smoothly to symmetrical musical strains. Its popularity swept 18th-century European ballrooms and fostered musical forms embraced by classical composers.
profile.profile_long:
The Angloise emerged from the international travels of English country dancing during the late seventeenth century. Although vernacular country dances had long circulated across the British Isles and were documented in John Playford's 1651 collection The English Dancing Master, their entry into Continental Europe marked an important stylistic transformation. Introduced to the court of Louis XIV of France in 1684, the dance came to be known as the anglaise or Angloise. French dancing masters initially used the designation loosely to describe various English folk dances, including the hornpipe, jig, and Scottish reel. Soon, however, court choreographers began systematically combining traditional English interactive patterns with French dance steps and baroque styling, giving rise to the formal contredanse.

Throughout the eighteenth century, the Angloise established itself across European ballrooms as a lively contrast to stately ceremonial displays like the minuet. André Lorin, returning from a diplomatic visit to the English court, presented Louis XIV with an annotated manuscript detailing dances in the English style. By 1706, Raoul Auger Feuillet published Recüeil de Contredances, which recorded contredanses anglaises in Beauchamp-Feuillet notation, incorporating both imported English routines and original French compositions. By the 1720s, the term contredanse settled heavily into longways sets divided into two- or three-couple minor sets, while square formations later evolved into the cotillion and quadrille. The dance flourished across Continental ballrooms until the close of the eighteenth century, leaving an extensive musical imprint on classical composers.

In structure, the Angloise relies on cooperative group floor patterns known as figures. Dancers assemble into sets—most frequently longways sets for 'as many as will' arranged in facing lines of couples, as well as squares of four couples. Unlike ballroom dances where couples dance independently or concert presentations like clogging, the Angloise is designed for broad social participation. Dancers trace floor paths described by period dancing master Thomas Wilson in 1820 as circular, half-circular, serpentine, angular, or straight lines. Through standard progressions, active couples move up or down the set so that participants interact with everyone over repeated iterations of the musical tune.

Musically, the dance is constructed to match symmetrical strains, historically written in 2/4 or 6/8 time. The most standard musical accompaniment consists of 32-bar tunes, typically jigs or reels. Its driving clarity and energetic phrasing led art music composers to adopt it as a distinct instrumental movement; both Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Ludwig van Beethoven incorporated the form into their works. By the early nineteenth century, the craze for the waltz and the quadrille began supplanting country dances in formal ballrooms, but the Angloise left an enduring legacy in regional folk forms, including Scandinavian engelska, Latin American contradanza, and modern contra dance.

sections.origins_and_history: Country dances originated in England and entered Continental courtly awareness in the late seventeenth century. The genre was introduced to the French court of Louis XIV in 1684 under the name anglaise. André Lorin visited the English court in the late seventeenth century and presented Louis XIV with a manuscript of dances in the English style upon his return. In 1706, Raoul Auger Feuillet published Recüeil de Contredances, documenting contredanses anglaises using Beauchamp-Feuillet notation. Through the French court, the style spread across Continental Europe, remaining popular among social dancers and composers through the late eighteenth century.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The Angloise is executed by sets of dancers who carry out predefined sequences of figures repeated over the course of a tune. Most commonly arranged in longways sets—two facing lines of partners—or four-couple squares, dancers progress through the set to interact with each couple. Figures trace circular, serpentine, angular, and straight lines on the floor, including simple communal movements like Circle Left and complex progressive figures such as Strip the Willow. The stepping and styling varied across regions, combining French court technique with English figures.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music for the dance is structured in fixed lengths to match the choreographic figures, most commonly 32-bar jigs or reels composed in 2/4 or 6/8 meter. Traditional, folk, and historical instrumental ensembles accompanied the dance. Classical composers embraced the form; Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart composed related dances such as 6 Ländlerische Tänze (K.606, dated 1791), and Ludwig van Beethoven produced works including the 6 Écossaises (WoO 83, dated 1806).
sections.costume_and_setting: Originally performed in seventeenth- and eighteenth-century European aristocratic courts and formal ballrooms, the dance functioned as a refreshing, energetic finale to social evenings dominated by stately dances such as the minuet. Historical clothing reflected court and ballroom attire of the eighteenth century.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The dance was conceived for broad social participation rather than solo spectacle. By allowing dancers to progress through the set and encounter every other couple, it created an egalitarian, interactive social atmosphere within structured ballroom etiquette.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures include King Louis XIV of France, who welcomed the dance to his court in 1684; André Lorin, who presented an English dance manuscript to the French monarch; Raoul Auger Feuillet, who published the 1706 notation manual Recüeil de Contredances; John Essex, who translated Feuillet's work into English; dance writer Thomas Wilson (1808, 1820); and classical composers Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart and Ludwig van Beethoven.
sections.regional_variants: Variants of the dance include the French contredanse, the Scandinavian Engelska (or Danish Engelsk, a 16-bar folk dance in 2/4), the Scottish écossaise, Irish set dance, New England contra dance, and the Spanish and Latin American contradanza.
sections.lineage: Emanating from English country dances documented in works such as John Playford's 1651 The English Dancing Master, the Angloise synthesized British country figures with French court dance. It subsequently gave rise to the eighteenth-century quadrille and cotillion, influenced the Latin American contradanza, and shaped modern contra dance traditions.

basic_steps: Stand in set formation facing partners or opposite lines
Trace circular path to the left (Circle Left)
Weave through opposite lines in progressive interaction (Strip the Willow)
Progress to new position in the set on the 32-bar cycle
teaching.formation: Longways sets of facing couples or four-couple squares
teaching.level_notes: Beginners start with simple intuitive floor paths such as circling before progressing to complex figures.

music_profile.musical_form: Symmetrical binary or multi-strain structure, most commonly 32 bars (jigs or reels)
music_profile.sound_description: Bright and rhythmic dance music organized into repeating strains, usually composed in 2/4 or 6/8 time. Designed to fit the length of dance figures, it commonly uses 32-bar structures characteristic of jigs and reels.

movement_profile.footwork: Regional and period-dependent stepping mixing English and French styling
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Longways sets for couples in lines or squares of four couples, tracing circular, serpentine, angular, and straight floor paths
movement_profile.partnering: Couples dancing interactive figures within a set with progressive movement

signature_moves.name: Circle Left
signature_moves.description: Intuitive circular floor pattern traced by dancers together in the set

signature_moves.name: Strip the Willow
signature_moves.description: Complex weaving figure executed across the set

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Dancing independently without regard to the set's progressive geometry

learning_units.description: Execute Circle Left smoothly within a set without breaking the circular line.
Perform the Strip the Willow weaving pattern across lines of partners.

prerequisites.description: Spatial awareness to maintain geometric floor patterns in longways and square sets.

feedback_rules.description: Identify failure to progress to the next position in the set during the 32-bar phrase iteration.

social_formats.description: Longways sets for as many couples as will, or squares composed of four couples.

activation_questions.question: Which specific French baroque dance steps (e.g., pas de bourrée, chassé) were integrated into the English figures described in Feuillet's 1706 Recüeil de Contredances?
activation_questions.why_needed: The source notes an experimentation of mixing English and French dance steps and styling, but does not name the discrete steps required for authentic instruction.
activation_questions.next_evidence: Consultation of Raoul Auger Feuillet's 1706 Recüeil de Contredances or John Essex's translation For the Further Improvement of Dancing.

episode_brief.title_hook: When English Country Lines Conquered the Court of Versailles
episode_brief.logline: Discover how a rustic English social dance transformed into the Angloise, captivating Louis XIV and redefining European ballrooms.
beats: Versailles, 1684: English country figures arrive at the court of the Sun King.
André Lorin presents an English dance manuscript to Louis XIV, sparking a courtly craze.
Raoul Auger Feuillet publishes his 1706 Recüeil, coding the Angloise in elegant notation.
Dancers demonstrate the geometric beauty of longways and square sets moving in synchrony.
The spread of the dance across Europe and its adoption into classical music by Mozart and Beethoven.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master set alignment and the basic Circle Left figure
drills: Establish longways facing lines with equal partner spacing
Walk a four-couple circle to the left returning to home spot
Practice rhythmic walking step to 32-bar musical phrasing

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute interactive couple figures and minor set changes
drills: Partner pass-through and cast off to adjacent set slot
Timing the 32-bar phrase to complete progression precisely on beat one

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute the intricate 'Strip the Willow' figure smoothly across the full line
drills: Top couple arm-turn drill progressing down alternating lines
Rejoining the bottom of the set without interrupting phrase tempo
Full set continuous progression drill through multiple tune repeats

visual_motifs: Geometric floor patterns filmed from overhead showing lines and squares
Pages from Feuillet's 1706 Beauchamp-Feuillet notation manual
Courtiers transitioning from rigid minuets to lively progressive country lines
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An articulate historical dance specialist who blends baroque court precision with communal warmth.
episode_brief.music_cue: A brisk 32-bar classical or early eighteenth-century contredanse tune in 2/4 meter.

seniors.seated_version: Perform arm-turns and progressive hand-clapping patterns in facing seated rows matching 32-bar phrasing.
seniors.standing_version: Gentle walking progression along longways lines, eliminating any quick footwork or sharp turns.
seniors.tempo_and_range: Moderate walking tempo with shortened floor travel distances.

children.game_version: Partner trading game where children navigate floor pathways like Circle Left and change spots each musical strain.

gaps: Specific historical baroque stepping techniques for the Angloise are not detailed in the sources.
